name: Synthesis Collective Biofilm Mask
description:
A full-face mask made from living biofilm substrate that bonds temporarily to the wearer's skin, creating a seamless, airtight seal. The biofilm filters airborne toxins, pathogens, and particulates while allowing normal respiration through engineered micropores. The mask is semi-transparent, giving the wearer's face a translucent, slightly unsettling appearance.

Developed for Synthesis Collective substrate handlers, the Biofilm Mask has become a status symbol in certain counter-culture circles where the organic-tech aesthetic carries ideological weight.
functionality: Airborne filtration, pathogen barrier, airtight seal, 48-hour active lifespan
what_it_says: You trust living technology more than dead machinery, and you want everyone to see that choice on your face.
story_hooks: A batch of Biofilm Masks begins bonding permanently to wearers' faces — the living substrate mutated, and removal now requires surgical intervention.

physical_description.visual_profile: A translucent, second-skin membrane covering the entire face from hairline to jaw. The biofilm gives the wearer an ethereal, slightly ghostly appearance—their features visible but softened and distorted through the semi-transparent organic layer. Creates an unsettling, almost alien visage that reads as both biological and technological.
physical_description.fit: Adheres directly to facial contours with a compression fit. The biofilm molds perfectly to individual facial geometry, creating zero gaps. Tight at cheekbones and temples, conforming seamlessly without restriction or discomfort.
physical_description.primary_material: Living biofilm substrate—engineered cellular matrix that bonds temporarily to epidermal layers. The substrate is semi-transparent with a faint iridescent quality.
physical_description.texture: Smooth and slightly wet to the touch, with a gel-like surface that catches light. Microporous structure is invisible to the naked eye but creates a subtle grainy appearance under magnification. The biofilm has a subtle breathing quality—slight undulations visible in certain light.
physical_description.color_scheme: Translucent pale amber with faint opalescent undertones. The wearer's natural skin tone visible beneath, creating a dual-layered color effect. Faint bioluminescent veining in pale green or cyan at the edges, especially visible in low light.
physical_description.closures: No traditional closures. The biofilm self-adheres to skin through organic bonding. Removal requires enzymatic solvent or natural degradation (12-18 hour lifespan). Seamless integration with the wearer's skin.
distinctive_features: Engineered micropore grid for filtered respiration—barely visible as ultra-fine patterning across the surface
Faint bioluminescent vessel patterns along cheekbones and jawline
Self-sealing around eyes, nostrils, and mouth—no visible gaps or edges
Subtle iridescence shifts color slightly depending on viewing angle
Synthesis Collective substrate handler certification marking on the right temple (small embossed certification seal)
physical_description.tier_indicator: Tier 2-3 boundary. Expensive medical-grade biotech (Tier 2 pricing) but widely adopted by working-class counter-culture (Tier 3 adoption). Signals insider status within Synthesis Collective or ideological alignment with organic-tech resistance movements.
physical_description.cultural_context: Worn by substrate handlers, biotech workers, environmental activists, and counter-culture figures who embrace human-ecosystem merger ideology. The mask signals rejection of chrome-heavy corpo aesthetics in favor of 'natural' augmentation philosophy. Also adopted by hazmat workers and those navigating contaminated zones.
physical_description.condition_typical: When fresh: pristine, barely visible, almost too seamless to notice. As it ages toward removal (12-18 hours): slight cloudiness, faint stress lines around high-movement areas (mouth, eyes), possible micro-tears. Worn masks show the wearer's face slightly more distinctly as the biofilm degrades.
